title: Kotlin Programming
description: Beginner-to-advanced Kotlin language reference covering syntax, types, null safety, functions, object modeling, generics, collections, delegation, DSLs, context parameters, coroutines, Flow, JVM interoperability, multiplatform development, testing, performance, tooling, and production API design.

sections.title: Getting Started, Platforms & Tooling
sections.description: Select a target and establish a reproducible build before adopting language features.

subtopics.title: Kotlin Targets & Platform Decision Guide
subtopics.description: Kotlin is a statically typed language compiled for JVM, JavaScript, Native, and Wasm, with Multiplatform source sets for shared code.

table.title: Kotlin Targets & Platform Decision Guide — production guide
rows: One language and type system can serve several deployment environments while retaining direct platform access.

Choose JVM for JVM ecosystems, JS for JavaScript integration, Native for native binaries or Apple/C interop, Wasm for supported portable workloads, and Multiplatform when substantial stable logic is genuinely shared.
Do not add Multiplatform solely to share a few models or when required libraries and operational expertise exist on only one target.
Target blocks select outputs; commonMain contains portable code and platform source sets contain target APIs. Compilation returns platform artifacts rather than one universal binary.
Runtime, startup, memory, build time, and interop costs differ by target; benchmark and operate the actual deployment artifact.
Java, Scala, JavaScript/TypeScript, Rust, Swift; related: source sets, expect/actual, interop.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Treating Multiplatform as write once, run everywhere and leaking platform APIs into common code.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Share stable domain rules first and keep UI, storage engines, networking clients, and lifecycle integration behind platform boundaries.

subtopics.title: Gradle, Toolchains & Compiler Options
subtopics.description: The Kotlin Gradle plugin coordinates compiler versions, target toolchains, dependencies, tests, and incremental compilation.

table.title: Gradle, Toolchains & Compiler Options — production guide
rows: Pinned, declarative builds make developer machines and CI compile the same source with the same language and runtime assumptions.
Use a version catalog or settings plugin management, explicit JVM toolchains, typed compilerOptions, dependency locking where appropriate, and wrapper-controlled Gradle.
Avoid relying on the IDE-bundled compiler, developer JAVA_HOME, dynamic dependency versions, or deprecated kotlinOptions configuration.
Plugin version selects Kotlin; jvmToolchain selects compiler JDK; jvmTarget selects bytecode. Gradle tasks return artifacts/reports and nonzero status on failure.
Compiler plugins and annotation/code generation can dominate build time; use build scans and incremental-build measurements before changing daemon settings.
Maven and command-line kotlinc are alternatives; related: version catalogs, toolchains, compilerOptions, dependencyInsight.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Confusing the compiler JDK, generated bytecode target, deployed JRE, and Kotlin language/API versions.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Upgrade Kotlin, Gradle, JDK, compiler plugins, and kotlinx libraries as a tested compatibility matrix.

subtopics.title: Packages, Files, Imports & Visibility
subtopics.description: Packages provide namespaces; files contain top-level declarations; imports resolve names; visibility limits who may depend on a declaration.

table.title: Packages, Files, Imports & Visibility — production guide
rows: Small, intentional module APIs reduce coupling and make compatibility and ownership reviewable.
Use cohesive files, explicit packages, private implementation details, internal module APIs, and explicit public signatures.
Avoid the default package, wildcard-heavy public code, Utils dumping grounds, and accidental public declarations.
package declares a namespace; import may use as aliases. Visibility is private, protected, internal, or public. Top-level functions return their declared or inferred type.
Visibility itself has negligible runtime cost, but a large public ABI increases compile invalidation, binary compatibility burden, and optimizer constraints.
Modules, interfaces, facade objects, package-level APIs; related: explicit API mode and binary compatibility.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example
tabs.code:
package com.example.orders

import java.time.Instant
import java.util.UUID as JavaUuid

private const val DEFAULT_LIMIT = 50

internal fun newId(): String = JavaUuid.randomUUID().toString()

public class OrderService(private val clock: () -> Instant)

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Assuming internal is a JVM security boundary; Java bytecode can still observe internal declarations.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Default to private/internal and publish only coherent contracts with explicit return types.

sections.title: Values, Types & Control Flow
sections.description: Prefer immutable values and expression-oriented control flow with explicit domain types.

subtopics.title: val, var, Constants & Type Inference
subtopics.description: val declares a read-only reference, var a reassignable reference, and const val a compile-time primitive or String constant.

table.title: val, var, Constants & Type Inference — production guide
rows: The compiler preserves static types while inference removes redundant syntax; read-only references reduce the number of possible state transitions.
Use val by default, var in a narrow owned scope, const val for annotation/compile-time values, and explicit types at public boundaries.
Avoid shared mutable var, uninitialized lateinit without lifecycle guarantees, and inferred public types that can change accidentally.
val name: Type = expression; var uses the same form and returns no value from assignment. lateinit supports non-null mutable properties; lazy returns a cached value on first access.
References add no special overhead. lazy may synchronize and retain its initializer/value; lateinit adds a runtime initialization check.
Immutable/persistent collections, atomic values, StateFlow; related: properties, delegates, concurrency.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example
tabs.code:
const val API_VERSION = "v1"
val count: Int = 3
var attempts = 0
attempts += 1

val index by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) {
    buildIndex()
}

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Believing val makes the referenced object immutable; a val MutableList can still be mutated.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Keep mutable ownership private and expose snapshots or read-only contracts.

subtopics.title: Numbers, Strings, Equality & Conversions
subtopics.description: Kotlin supplies signed and unsigned numeric types, immutable strings, explicit numeric conversions, structural equality with ==, and identity equality with ===.

table.title: Numbers, Strings, Equality & Conversions — production guide
rows: Explicit conversions prevent silent precision loss, while distinct equality operators separate value semantics from object identity.
Use == for values, === only for identity invariants, string templates for formatting, buildString for loops, and BigDecimal or integer minor units for money on JVM.
Avoid Double for money, reference equality for strings, implicit locale assumptions, and repeated string concatenation in large loops.
toInt/toLong and parsing functions return converted values or throw; toIntOrNull returns Int?. == returns Boolean and is null-safe; === returns Boolean identity.
Primitive arrays avoid boxing. Generic/nullable/value-class contexts may box. buildString avoids repeated intermediate String allocation.
BigInteger, BigDecimal, value classes, locale APIs; related: data classes and serialization.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Constructing BigDecimal from a Double preserves the binary approximation; construct it from a String or integer representation.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Make units and precision part of domain types and specify locale/charset at external boundaries.

subtopics.title: if, when, Loops, Ranges & Destructuring
subtopics.description: if, when, and try are expressions; loops are statements; ranges/progressions describe ordered iteration; destructuring calls component functions.

table.title: if, when, Loops, Ranges & Destructuring — production guide
rows: Expression-oriented code makes branch results explicit and sealed/enum when expressions compiler-checkable.
Use if for two branches, exhaustive when for closed variants, for for visible control flow, and destructuring for small stable tuples/data classes.
Avoid fragile else branches over owned sealed types, non-local returns hidden in forEach, large destructuring declarations, and ranges with incorrect inclusive bounds.
if/when/try return the common branch type. for/while/repeat return Unit. .. includes the end; until excludes it; downTo and step create progressions.
Primitive progressions are efficient. Destructuring may call unused component functions unless skipped with _, and collection chains may allocate.
Collection operators, sequences, sealed types, enum entries, guard clauses; related: labels and smart casts.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: A bare return inside inline forEach returns from the enclosing function; use a for loop when break, continue, or return semantics matter.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Omit else for owned closed hierarchies so a new case produces compiler errors at every incomplete decision.

sections.title: Null Safety, Failures & Contracts
sections.description: Represent ordinary absence, exceptional failure, and invariant violations with distinct mechanisms.

subtopics.title: Nullable Types, Safe Calls & Elvis
subtopics.description: T? admits null while T does not; safe calls propagate null and Elvis supplies a fallback or exits.

table.title: Nullable Types, Safe Calls & Elvis — production guide
rows: Nullability in the type system moves many missing-value defects to compile time and makes absence visible at call sites.
Use nullable types for expected absence, ?. for propagation, ?: for defaults/early returns, and requireNotNull/checkNotNull at proven boundaries.
Avoid !!, long safe-call chains that hide which value is missing, and nullable fields when a sealed state better explains lifecycle.
value?.member returns a nullable member result; value ?: fallback returns a common branch type; value!! returns T or throws; let transforms a non-null receiver.
Null-safety operators are generally cheap; repeated chains may duplicate work if expressions are not stored. Boxing can occur for nullable primitives/value classes.
Sealed states, Option-like domain types, getOrNull, mapNotNull; related: platform types and smart casts.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example
tabs.code:
fun displayName(user: User?): String =
    user?.profile?.name?.trim()
        ?.takeIf(String::isNotEmpty)
        ?: "Anonymous"

fun requireToken(headers: Map<String, String>): String =
    requireNotNull(headers["Authorization"])

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Letting Java platform types T! spread through Kotlin code without validation can reintroduce NPEs despite apparently non-null declarations.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Normalize platform and deserialization values at the boundary, then keep domain code non-null where invariants require it.

subtopics.title: Exceptions, Result & Typed Domain Errors
subtopics.description: Kotlin exceptions are unchecked; Result<T> wraps success or Throwable failure; sealed outcomes encode expected domain failures.

table.title: Exceptions, Result & Typed Domain Errors — production guide
rows: Different failure representations tell callers whether absence is normal, recovery is required, or execution cannot continue.
Use T? for reasonless absence, a sealed result for expected business outcomes, Result at exception-adapting boundaries, and throw for violated contracts or operation failures.
Avoid exceptions for normal branching, Result everywhere, swallowing causes, and exposing infrastructure exception classes as a domain API.
throw has type Nothing; try is an expression; runCatching returns Result<T>; getOrElse/fold transform it. A sealed when returns the selected response.
Exceptions are cheap when not thrown but stack traces are expensive. Typed results allocate objects but can make routine outcomes explicit and benchmarkable.
Nullable return, sealed interface, Either libraries, require/check; related: cancellation and HTTP error mapping.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Catching Throwable or Exception inside a coroutine and failing to rethrow CancellationException breaks structured cancellation.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Translate failures once at an ownership boundary, preserve the original cause, add safe operation context, and log only where recovery/response ownership exists.

subtopics.title: Preconditions, Assertions & Contracts
subtopics.description: require validates caller input, check validates state, error marks impossible paths, assertions support development checks, and contracts describe call effects to the compiler.

table.title: Preconditions, Assertions & Contracts — production guide
rows: Specific invariant APIs communicate responsibility and improve smart-cast/data-flow reasoning.
Use require/requireNotNull at API boundaries, check/checkNotNull for internal state, error for unreachable paths, and standard contracts through standard-library helpers.
Avoid assert for security/correctness because JVM assertions may be disabled, and avoid custom contracts unless their semantics are small, stable, and proven.
require returns Unit or throws IllegalArgumentException; check returns Unit or throws IllegalStateException; requireNotNull/checkNotNull return non-null T; error returns Nothing.
Lazy message lambdas run only on failure. Exceptions and stack traces dominate failure cost, so do not use invariant failures as a hot-path control mechanism.
Factory functions, sealed validation errors, Result, smart casts; related: contracts and value classes.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Using require for malformed external payloads without converting the exception into a safe client-facing error leaks implementation-oriented failure handling.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Validate untrusted input into an explicit error model, then construct types that cannot represent invalid state.

sections.title: Functions & Functional Programming
sections.description: Treat functions as explicit contracts and use higher-order abstractions only where behavior stays visible.

subtopics.title: Functions, Parameters, Defaults & Returns
subtopics.description: Functions declare named typed parameters and a return type; expression bodies infer returns; named/default arguments improve call-site clarity.

table.title: Functions, Parameters, Defaults & Returns — production guide
rows: A clear signature exposes required input, optional policy, output, side effects, and failure ownership.
Use explicit return types for public APIs, named arguments for ambiguous literals, defaults for stable common policy, and vararg only for small ergonomic lists.
Avoid boolean blindness, default expressions that perform I/O, enormous parameter lists, and relying on Java parameter names as a compatibility guarantee.
fun name(p: T = default): R; parameters are evaluated left-to-right. Assignment returns Unit. Unit means no meaningful value; Nothing means normal return is impossible.
Default/named arguments are primarily compile-time features. vararg creates an array; spreading an existing array can copy.
Builder, parameter object, overload, extension function; related: ABI compatibility and Java @JvmOverloads.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Changing a default parameter can alter behavior after recompilation while existing compiled consumers may retain prior call-site behavior.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Use parameter objects when related options evolve together and domain types instead of multiple same-typed primitives.

subtopics.title: Lambdas, Function Types & Higher-Order Functions
subtopics.description: Function types such as (T) -> R represent executable behavior; lambdas and callable references create values of those types.

table.title: Lambdas, Function Types & Higher-Order Functions — production guide
rows: Higher-order functions separate reusable control flow from a small injected policy or transformation.
Use lambdas for local behavior, callable references for existing functions, receiver lambdas for focused builders, and fun interface for a named single-method contract.
Avoid capturing large/short-lived objects in long-lived callbacks, nested receiver ambiguity, and using a function type for an evolving multi-operation service.
(A, B) -> R accepts two parameters and returns R; suspend (T) -> R may suspend; T.() -> R supplies T as receiver; invoking returns the lambda result.
Capturing lambdas may allocate and retain captured state. Inline higher-order functions can remove allocation but may increase code size.
Named function, fun interface, interface, strategy object; related: inline, receiver DSLs, callable references.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Using map for side effects creates and discards a result list; use forEach or an explicit loop.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Name complex lambdas, keep them short, and define callback lifetime/unregistration when ownership crosses components.

subtopics.title: inline, reified, noinline, crossinline & tailrec
subtopics.description: Inlining copies eligible function/lambda code at call sites; reified exposes an inline type argument; noinline preserves a lambda object; crossinline forbids non-local returns; tailrec rewrites eligible recursion.

table.title: inline, reified, noinline, crossinline & tailrec — production guide
rows: These modifiers enable type-safe runtime checks, non-local control flow, or lower hot-path lambda overhead when semantics require them.
Use small inline higher-order utilities, reified adapters/lookups, noinline for stored lambdas, crossinline for deferred invocation, and tailrec only for truly tail-recursive algorithms.
Avoid marking normal functions inline as ritual, large public inline bodies, reified as a reflection framework, and deep non-tail recursion.
inline fun <reified T> returns the declared R; reified T supports is T and T::class. noinline/crossinline apply to lambda parameters. tailrec must call itself in tail position.
Inlining trades dispatch/allocation for duplicated bytecode or target code. Measure runtime and artifact size; tailrec avoids stack growth only when compiler eligibility is met.
KClass tokens, ordinary generic function, loop, compiler specialization; related: erasure and binary compatibility.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Forgetting that public inline bodies become part of consumer binaries and cannot freely reference non-public declarations.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Keep public inline APIs small and stable; use @PublishedApi only for deliberate internal helpers.

sections.title: Classes, Objects & Domain Modeling
sections.description: Encode invariants in small types and use composition or closed hierarchies to constrain state.

subtopics.title: Classes, Constructors, Members & Inheritance
subtopics.description: Classes are final by default; a primary constructor lives in the header; init blocks and property initializers run in source order.

table.title: Classes, Constructors, Members & Inheritance — production guide
rows: Final-by-default classes protect invariants, while intentional constructors and factories control valid state creation.
Use private constructors plus factories for validation, open/abstract only for designed extension points, and composition for code reuse.
Avoid calling open members during construction, inheriting merely to reuse code, and exposing mutable setters for invariant-rich state.
class C(val x: T) constructs C; init returns Unit; functions return declared values. open permits override, abstract requires implementation, super delegates to a base constructor/member.
Virtual dispatch has small runtime cost; object design, allocation, cache locality, and framework proxies matter more. Factories may enable pooling/caching only when measured and safe.
Factory function, sealed hierarchy, interface/delegation, composition; related: visibility and properties.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Calling an open property or function from init can dispatch into a subclass before subclass state is initialized.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Make invalid states unconstructable and expose behavioral methods rather than mutable data bags.

subtopics.title: data, enum, value, object & data object
subtopics.description: Special class forms generate or constrain semantics: data classes model transparent values, enums fixed singleton choices, value classes typed scalar wrappers, and objects single instances.

table.title: data, enum, value, object & data object — production guide
rows: They reduce boilerplate while making equality, allowed cases, representation, and lifecycle explicit.
Use immutable data classes for records, enum for uniform fixed constants, value class for IDs/units, object for stateless singleton behavior, and data object for singleton sealed cases.
Avoid data classes for mutable identity entities, enums for payload-diverse variants, value classes where identity/boxing/interop dominates, and objects as global mutable service locators.
data generates equals/hashCode/toString/copy/componentN from primary properties; enum entries are instances; value class wraps one val; object returns the singleton reference.
Value classes are often unboxed but box in nullable, generic, interface, and some interop contexts. data operations traverse referenced property equality/hash behavior.
Regular class, sealed variants, typealias, dependency-injected singleton; related: equality, serialization, boxing.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: data class copy is shallow and body properties do not participate in generated equality or copy.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Keep data-class primary properties immutable, validate value-class input, and never place secrets in generated toString output.

subtopics.title: Interfaces, Sealed Hierarchies & Delegation
subtopics.description: Interfaces define open behavioral contracts, sealed types restrict direct variants, and by delegation forwards an interface implementation to a collaborator.

table.title: Interfaces, Sealed Hierarchies & Delegation — production guide
rows: These tools separate capabilities, closed domain states, and reusable composition without deep inheritance.
Use interfaces for third-party implementations, sealed types for exhaustive outcomes/events, and delegation for decorators or selective overrides.
Avoid sealed types for plugin extension points, broad marker interfaces, and delegation that hides unclear ownership or an oversized contract.
interface members return declared types; sealed subclasses must satisfy permitted-location rules; class Wrapper(d: I) : I by d forwards calls and may override selected members.
Interface dispatch is typically cheap relative to I/O. Delegation adds an object/reference layer; sealed exhaustiveness has compile-time benefit and no required reflection.
Abstract class, enum, composition, visitor; related: polymorphism, state machines, decorators.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Adding else to an owned sealed when suppresses compiler guidance when a new case is introduced.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Prefer small role interfaces and exhaustive when without else in code that owns the hierarchy.

sections.title: Generics, Variance & Runtime Types
sections.description: Preserve type relationships statically while accounting for erasure and platform interop.

subtopics.title: Generics, Bounds, in/out Variance & Projections
subtopics.description: Generics parameterize types; out marks producers, in marks consumers, invariance allows both, bounds require capabilities, and star projections represent an unknown safe type.

table.title: Generics, Bounds, in/out Variance & Projections — production guide
rows: Variance allows safe substitution without casts and documents whether a contract reads or writes values.
Use declaration-site variance on owned producer/consumer interfaces, where clauses for multiple bounds, and use-site projections to adapt invariant APIs.
Avoid variance when the type is both consumed and produced, unchecked casts, and star projections when the concrete relationship matters.
C<T> is invariant; Source<out T> may return T; Sink<in T> may accept T; where T : A constrains inputs and returns preserve T relationships.
Generics are commonly erased on JVM and can box primitives/value classes; specialized primitive collections/arrays may matter in measured hot paths.
Non-generic interface, sealed variants, primitive arrays, use-site projections; related: Java wildcards and reified.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Declaring out on a type later expected to consume T forces unsafe workarounds and signals the abstraction was not actually producer-only.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Apply producer out, consumer in, keep mutable containers invariant, and test Java-facing wildcard signatures.

subtopics.title: Type Checks, Casts, Smart Casts & Type Aliases
subtopics.description: is performs a runtime check, as casts or throws, as? casts or returns null, smart casts narrow stable values, and typealias gives an existing type another source-level name.

table.title: Type Checks, Casts, Smart Casts & Type Aliases — production guide
rows: These features bridge open/runtime data into statically known branches while aliases improve readability without creating new types.
Use is in closed boundary dispatch, as? for optional matches, guard clauses for smart casts, and typealias for complex callback/generic names.
Avoid as on untrusted data, repetitive type switching instead of polymorphism, aliases for domain separation, and assumptions that erased generic arguments can be checked.
x is T returns Boolean; x as T returns T or throws ClassCastException; x as? T returns T?; typealias creates no wrapper/runtime type.
Runtime checks and casts are usually small but type-switch-heavy designs impede optimization and extensibility. Aliases cost nothing because they create no type.
Polymorphism, sealed when, value class, reified type parameter; related: erasure and platform types.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Mutable, open, or captured properties may change between check and use and therefore cannot always be smart-cast.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Copy unstable properties to a local val and validate dynamic payloads once into owned typed models.

subtopics.title: Annotations, Reflection & Opt-In
subtopics.description: Annotations attach compiler/tool/runtime metadata; reflection inspects types dynamically; opt-in markers flag unstable or delicate contracts.

table.title: Annotations, Reflection & Opt-In — production guide
rows: Frameworks and tooling need declarative metadata, while opt-in makes stability risk explicit at compile time.
Use narrow targets/retention, explicit use-site targets for JVM frameworks, generated code for hot mappings, and RequiresOptIn for genuinely unstable APIs.
Avoid runtime retention without a consumer, reflection in hot/startup-sensitive paths without measurement, and experimental APIs in stable public signatures.
Annotation parameters are compile-time constants; KClass identifies a type; reflection calls return metadata/results or throw; @OptIn accepts marker KClass values and returns no runtime result.
Reflection can increase startup, retained metadata, artifact size, and shrinker configuration. Generated codecs/adapters move failures to compile time.
KSP/code generation, compiler plugin, explicit registry, service loader; related: serialization and dependency injection.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Assuming a Kotlin property annotation reaches the Java field/getter location expected by a framework; use field:, get:, param:, or all: deliberately.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Verify generated bytecode/metadata for interop and document stability plus migration expectations for opt-in APIs.

sections.title: Collections, Sequences & Data Processing
sections.description: Choose structures by semantics and complexity, then keep data pipelines bounded and explicit.

subtopics.title: List, Set, Map, Arrays & Mutability
subtopics.description: Lists preserve order and duplicates, sets enforce uniqueness, maps associate keys, arrays have fixed size, and mutable variants permit structural changes.

table.title: List, Set, Map, Arrays & Mutability — production guide
rows: The right structure communicates invariants and controls lookup, insertion, memory, boxing, and iteration behavior.
Use List for ordered results, Set for membership, Map for stable-key lookup, primitive arrays for numeric buffers, and private mutable builders for owned construction.
Avoid exposing mutable collections, mutable map keys, relying on unspecified hash iteration order, and assuming read-only interfaces are deeply immutable.
Index/get returns an element or may throw; getOrNull returns T?; map lookup returns V?; add/remove on mutable collections return Boolean or removed value depending on API.
List index is O(1) and search O(n); hash Set/Map lookup is average O(1); primitive arrays avoid boxing; copying snapshots costs O(n).
Persistent immutable collections, ArrayDeque, sorted maps/sets, sequences; related: value semantics and concurrency.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: A List<T> may reference a MutableList<T> changed elsewhere; read-only is not a deep immutability guarantee.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Keep mutation behind one owner, copy at trust/concurrency boundaries, and document ordering and duplicate-key policies.

subtopics.title: Transform, Filter, Group, Associate & Fold
subtopics.description: Collection operators declaratively transform, select, index, partition, and aggregate finite data.

table.title: Transform, Filter, Group, Associate & Fold — production guide
rows: Named operators make common O(n) pipelines concise and composable while preserving types.
Use map for one output per input, mapNotNull for optional output, groupingBy for per-key aggregates, associateBy for an explicit last-value-wins index, and fold with an identity.
Avoid map for side effects, reduce on possibly empty input, repeated scans in hot paths, and silent associateBy duplicate loss.
map(transform: (T)->R) returns List<R>; filter(predicate) returns List<T>; groupBy returns Map<K,List<T>>; fold(initial, operation) returns accumulator R.
Eager intermediate operators allocate collections. groupingBy can aggregate without building a List for every key; mapTo/filterTo reuse caller-owned destinations.
Explicit loop, Sequence, Flow, database query; related: aggregation, complexity, allocation.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example
tabs.code:
data class Order(val customerId: CustomerId, val total: Money)

val totals: Map<CustomerId, Money> = orders
    .groupingBy(Order::customerId)
    .fold(Money.ZERO) { sum, order -> sum + order.total }

val duplicateIds = users.groupingBy(User::id)
    .eachCount()
    .filterValues { it > 1 }
    .keys

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: associateBy keeps the later element for duplicate keys; if duplicates mean corruption, detect and reject them explicitly.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Keep short pipelines readable, name nontrivial predicates/transforms, and document empty-input and duplicate behavior.

subtopics.title: Sequence Laziness & Allocation Decisions
subtopics.description: Sequence is a synchronous lazy pull pipeline that evaluates intermediate operations per element at a terminal operation.

table.title: Sequence Laziness & Allocation Decisions — production guide
rows: It can avoid intermediate lists and stop upstream early for long multi-stage or short-circuiting pipelines.
Use Sequence for measured large chains, take/first short-circuiting, or a source naturally consumed once.
Avoid it for small/simple list operations, repeated side-effectful iteration, asynchronous streams, or resources whose closure is unclear.
asSequence returns Sequence<T>; intermediate operators return another Sequence; terminal toList/first/fold returns a materialized value and triggers evaluation.
Benefits depend on input size, operator count, short-circuit position, and target. Benchmark end-to-end with JMH or the target profiler.
Iterable operators, explicit loop, Flow for asynchronous values; related: laziness, terminal operations, benchmarking.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example
tabs.code:
val firstTen = records.asSequence()
    .filter(Record::isActive)
    .mapNotNull(Record::email)
    .distinct()
    .take(10)
    .toList()

// Simpler for a small list and one operation:
val active = records.filter(Record::isActive)

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Assuming lazy automatically means faster; iterator, lambda, boxing, and virtual-call overhead can exceed saved allocation.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Start with direct collection operators, switch only when workload evidence and readability support it.

sections.title: Extensions, Properties & DSLs
sections.description: Use concise syntax while keeping receivers, evaluation, side effects, and dependency scope visible.

subtopics.title: Extensions & Scope Functions
subtopics.description: Extensions add statically dispatched member-like syntax; let/run/with/apply/also differ by receiver name and returned value.

table.title: Extensions & Scope Functions — production guide
rows: They enable focused adapters, null transforms, initialization, and side-effect taps without wrapper boilerplate.
Use let for nullable transforms, run for receiver computation, apply for configuration, also for a small side effect, and extensions for cohesive convenience.
Avoid nested scope functions, ambiguous this/it, long workflows hidden in apply/also, and extensions that pretend to override runtime behavior.
let/also pass it; run/with/apply use this. let/run/with return lambda result; apply/also return receiver. Extension receiver is resolved from compile-time type.
Extensions usually compile like static functions. Scope lambdas may allocate unless inlined; readability and captured lifetime are usually the larger risks.
Member function, top-level function, adapter/decorator; related: static dispatch, nullable let, receiver lambdas.

fun String.toSlug(): String = trim()
    .lowercase()
    .replace(Regex("[^a-z0-9]+"), "-")
    .trim('-')

val client = HttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(5.seconds)
    .build()
    .also { logger.info("HTTP client created") }

val length = text?.let(String::length) ?: 0

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: A member with the same signature always wins, and an extension selected from a base-typed reference does not dynamically dispatch to a subtype extension.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Use at most one short scope function at a time and name the receiver explicitly when meaning is not obvious.

subtopics.title: Properties, Accessors, Delegates & Backing Fields
subtopics.description: Properties expose get/set semantics, custom accessors compute or validate values, delegates reuse storage behavior, and backing fields store property state.

table.title: Properties, Accessors, Delegates & Backing Fields — production guide
rows: They let APIs express value access while centralizing initialization, observation, validation, or shared storage rules.
Use cheap deterministic computed properties, private setters for owned mutation, lazy for one-time deferred work, and delegates for repeated well-understood property policy.
Avoid I/O or expensive failure-prone work in getters, delegated global state, and assuming lazy always retries or always has desired thread semantics.
get returns property T; set(value: T) returns Unit. by lazy returns cached T; observable callback receives property, old, new; explicit field syntax controls storage in Kotlin 2.4.
Custom getters run on every access; lazy retains its result and may synchronize; observable invokes callbacks on each assignment.
Explicit field, factory, cached function, StateFlow; related: lateinit, lazy modes, delegation.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Hiding network, disk, blocking, or large allocation work behind property access violates caller expectations and complicates failure handling.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Use a function when an operation is expensive, suspending, side-effecting, or can meaningfully fail.

subtopics.title: Operators, Infix Calls, DSLs & Context Parameters
subtopics.description: Operator/infix functions provide domain notation, receiver lambdas build type-safe DSLs, and stable Kotlin 2.4 context parameters supply lexical capabilities.

table.title: Operators, Infix Calls, DSLs & Context Parameters — production guide
rows: These features can remove repetitive plumbing when the notation has one unsurprising meaning and the dependency scope remains visible.
Use conventional operators, small infix relations, DslMarker-protected builders, and context parameters for tightly scoped cross-cutting capabilities.
Avoid surprising operator side effects, long infix chains, nested same-type receivers, hidden global-like dependencies, and experimental explicit context arguments in stable APIs.
operator functions use prescribed names/signatures and return their declared type; infix requires one parameter; T.() -> R returns R; context(name: Type) adds required lexical parameters.
DSL and context abstraction is mostly compile-time, but lambdas/captures and expanded code can allocate or enlarge artifacts; benchmark generated hot builders.
Named methods, builder object, explicit parameter, dependency injection; related: receivers, DslMarker, context functions.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Multiple implicit receivers or context values can make name resolution and overload selection unclear.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Keep experimental context arguments and callable-reference forms out of stable public APIs; prefer constructor or explicit parameter injection when ownership matters.

sections.title: Coroutines, Flow & Concurrency
sections.description: Give every concurrent task an owner, cancellation path, capacity limit, and observable failure policy.

subtopics.title: suspend, Coroutine Scopes, launch & async
subtopics.description: A suspend function may pause without blocking its thread; structured scopes bind child lifetimes to a parent; launch returns Job and async returns Deferred<T>.

table.title: suspend, Coroutine Scopes, launch & async — production guide
rows: Structured lifetime ownership prevents leaked background work and makes failure/cancellation propagation predictable.
Use suspend for asynchronous single results, coroutineScope for parallel children, launch for owned no-result work, and async only for concurrently computed values.
Avoid GlobalScope, internally unowned scopes, async followed immediately by await, and assuming suspend automatically switches threads.
suspend function parameters/return are source-level contracts; launch returns Job; async returns Deferred<T>; await returns T or propagates failure; coroutineScope returns block R.
Coroutines are lightweight, not free; unbounded fan-out consumes memory, connections, rate limits, and dispatcher capacity.
Synchronous function, CompletableFuture/Promise, executor; related: Job hierarchy, supervisorScope, cancellation.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Starting work in an application-wide scope for a request/component operation allows it to outlive its owner and lose errors.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Inject/own scopes at lifecycle boundaries and bound concurrency according to downstream capacity.

subtopics.title: Dispatchers, Cancellation, Timeouts & Supervision
subtopics.description: Dispatchers select execution resources; cancellation cooperatively propagates through Jobs; timeouts cancel waiting; supervision isolates sibling failures.

table.title: Dispatchers, Cancellation, Timeouts & Supervision — production guide
rows: Explicit execution and failure policy keeps CPU work, blocking I/O, cleanup, and partial-failure behavior controlled.
Use Default for CPU work, IO for blocking JVM I/O, ensureActive in long loops, withTimeout for bounded waits, and supervisorScope only when each child result/failure is handled.
Avoid hard-coded dispatchers deep in business code, swallowing CancellationException, NonCancellable around normal work, and treating timeout as remote rollback.
withContext returns block R; withTimeout returns R or throws TimeoutCancellationException; ensureActive returns Unit or throws cancellation; supervisorScope returns block R.
Context switching and scheduling have cost; blocking calls can exhaust pools; timeouts create cancellation/cleanup work and do not undo external side effects.
Executor, virtual threads, reactive runtime; related: CancellationException, Semaphore, supervisorScope.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Catching Exception broadly and returning a fallback can convert cancellation into success and keep unwanted work alive.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Catch only recoverable exceptions, use try/finally for cleanup, and design timed-out external operations for idempotency and reconciliation.

subtopics.title: Flow, StateFlow, SharedFlow & Channels
subtopics.description: Flow is usually cold asynchronous data, StateFlow is hot conflated state, SharedFlow is configurable broadcast, and Channel is a queue-like communication primitive.

table.title: Flow, StateFlow, SharedFlow & Channels — production guide
rows: Distinct stream types make execution, replay, ownership, fan-out, and slow-consumer policy explicit.
Use Flow for queries/transformations, StateFlow for current state, SharedFlow for broadcast events with deliberate replay/buffer, and Channel for internal work distribution.
Avoid StateFlow for non-conflatable events, Channel as a general public event API, endless flows where a suspend result suffices, and undocumented overflow/drop policy.
collect consumes and returns Unit; first returns T; stateIn returns StateFlow<T>; shareIn returns SharedFlow<T>; send suspends/returns Unit; receive returns T.
Operator chains allocate/cancel work; replay retains values; high-frequency streams and slow collectors need measured capacity and payload size.
Suspend function, Sequence, callback, reactive streams; related: backpressure, stateIn, shareIn, channelFlow.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Adding buffer, conflate, collectLatest, or DROP_OLDEST for performance without deciding which domain values may be lost.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Expose StateFlow/SharedFlow, keep mutable variants private, and test subscription, cancellation, replay, and slow-consumer behavior.

sections.title: JVM Interop, Multiplatform & Serialization
sections.description: Design explicit boundaries for runtime platforms, foreign callers, and wire schemas.

subtopics.title: Java Interoperability & JVM API Design
subtopics.description: Kotlin/JVM directly consumes Java types and emits JVM bytecode; annotations shape static access, overloads, fields, names, and checked-exception declarations for Java callers.

table.title: Java Interoperability & JVM API Design — production guide
rows: Kotlin conveniences do not always produce an ergonomic or compatible Java API, so foreign-facing surfaces need deliberate design.
Use recognized Java nullability annotations, adapters for platform types, @JvmOverloads selectively, @JvmStatic for intended static entry points, and @Throws for checked Java contracts.
Avoid leaking function types, default-only signatures, unsigned/value-class surprises, Unit, or Kotlin collection mutability ambiguity without testing Java callers.
@JvmOverloads emits trailing-default overloads; @JvmStatic emits a static bridge; @Throws writes throws metadata; @JvmName changes JVM name; functions return JVM-mapped values.
Interop bridges/boxing may affect hot APIs, but correctness and stable signatures matter first. Inspect bytecode and benchmark representative Java calls.
Java facade, overloads, SAM interface, generated adapter; related: wildcards, erasure, value classes.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Trusting a Java platform type as non-null and allowing a distant Kotlin NPE instead of validating at the adapter boundary.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Compile tests written in Java against every public JVM library API and keep platform types out of the domain layer.

subtopics.title: Multiplatform Source Sets & expect/actual
subtopics.description: Multiplatform source sets group portable and target-specific code; expect declares a common platform contract and actual supplies target implementations.

table.title: Multiplatform Source Sets & expect/actual — production guide
rows: The hierarchy shares tested logic while preserving direct access to each platform where abstractions would be leaky.
Use commonMain for pure/shared library code, interfaces plus injection for service behavior, expect/actual for small stable platform declarations, and platform sets for OS/framework integration.
Avoid large expect/actual service surfaces, platform assumptions in common code, publishing untested targets, and manual source-set hierarchies without real shared behavior.
expect and actual declarations must match; interfaces return owned common types; target blocks produce separate artifacts; commonTest uses kotlin.test.
Every target adds compilation, publication, CI, and support cost. Native linking and platform interop can dominate build time.
Separate platform projects, code generation, C/Swift/JS interop; related: source-set hierarchy and dependency variants.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Compiling only the primary target in CI allows actual declarations, dependencies, and tests on secondary targets to silently rot.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Define supported target tiers, compile/test each published target, and keep shared code dependent only on supported multiplatform libraries.

subtopics.title: Serialization & External Data Boundaries
subtopics.description: Serialization maps typed wire models to formats such as JSON; kotlinx.serialization generates multiplatform codecs from explicit metadata.

table.title: Serialization & External Data Boundaries — production guide
rows: A deliberate wire schema separates untrusted/evolving external data from invariant-rich domain objects.
Use dedicated payload types, stable serial names, bounded decoding, explicit unknown/null/default policy, allowlisted polymorphism, and mapping validation.
Avoid serializing domain internals blindly, arbitrary class-name polymorphism, unbounded payloads, platform-default time/charset, and secrets in generated toString/logs.
encodeToString returns String; decodeFromString<T> returns T or throws SerializationException; @SerialName sets wire key; serializer selection determines supported types.
Generated codecs usually outperform reflection but payload size/depth and large intermediate strings still dominate memory and latency.
Jackson/Moshi on JVM, Protobuf, manual codecs; related: schema evolution, sealed polymorphism, security.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Treating missing and explicit null as universally equivalent can erase patch semantics and backward-compatibility information.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Validate size and domain invariants before use, redact diagnostics, and test old/new payload compatibility plus hostile inputs.

sections.title: Testing, APIs & Production Engineering
sections.description: Turn behavior, compatibility, performance, security, and observability into executable build policies.

subtopics.title: Unit, Integration, Coroutine & Multiplatform Tests
subtopics.description: kotlin.test provides portable assertions while target runners execute tests; coroutine tests use a controlled scheduler and scope.

table.title: Unit, Integration, Coroutine & Multiplatform Tests — production guide
rows: Layered tests verify pure rules, boundary integration, implementation contracts, concurrency, and platform behavior without coupling every test to internals.
Use unit tests for pure behavior, integration tests for real boundaries, shared contract suites for implementations, runTest for coroutines, and target tests for platform physics.
Avoid testing private lines, sleep-based timing, mocking the system under integration, hard-coded Dispatchers, and collecting infinite flows without bounds/background ownership.
@Test functions return Unit; assertions either return Unit or throw AssertionError; assertFailsWith<T> returns caught T; runTest supplies TestScope and virtual time.
Test runtime is controlled mostly by I/O, framework startup, fixtures, and parallelism. Keep unit tests deterministic and profile slow suites rather than adding arbitrary concurrency.
JUnit, Kotest, property testing, Testcontainers, JMH; related: fakes, virtual time, contract tests.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: An endless Flow collected in the main runTest body prevents the test from completing; use take, first, or backgroundScope with cancellation.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Inject clocks, randomness, dispatchers/scopes, and owned ports; test observable contracts and cancellation/failure paths.

subtopics.title: Public API, Modules & Binary Compatibility
subtopics.description: Library evolution includes source, binary, behavioral, serialization, and multiplatform compatibility; explicit API mode forces public visibility and types.

table.title: Public API, Modules & Binary Compatibility — production guide
rows: Consumers compile against signatures and may inline bodies/default behavior, so seemingly small changes can break old binaries or newly compiled source.
Use explicitApi, ABI validation, semantic versioning, replacement APIs, deprecation cycles, and tests from representative Kotlin/Java consumers.
Avoid leaking dependency types, changing return/signature types in place, removing deprecated APIs immediately, and assuming default parameters preserve binary compatibility.
Public functions/properties form ABI; @Deprecated supplies message/ReplaceWith/level; explicitApi requires visibility/return declarations. Build validation returns failure on ABI drift.
Large public ABI increases incremental compilation and compatibility tooling work; public inline code duplicates into consumers and constrains internal evolution.
New method/name, overload bridge, facade, adapter; related: semantic versioning, Maven publication, @PublishedApi.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Adding a defaulted parameter or changing an inline body is not automatically safe for already-compiled consumers.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Keep public surface small, document compatibility guarantees per target, and test both fresh source compilation and old-binary linkage.

subtopics.title: Performance, Security & Observability
subtopics.description: Production quality depends on measured runtime/build behavior, bounded resource use, validated inputs, redacted telemetry, and target-appropriate profiling.

table.title: Performance, Security & Observability — production guide
rows: Language safety does not prevent excessive allocation, blocking, queue growth, injection, path traversal, SSRF, ReDoS, or secret leakage.
Profile realistic workloads, bound concurrency/retries/payloads, validate URLs/paths/ranges, use structured low-cardinality telemetry, and scan dependencies/secrets.
Avoid wall-clock microbenchmarks in main, logging raw payloads/tokens, unbounded async fan-out, high-cardinality metric labels, and speculative allocation rewrites.
Profilers/benchmarks return measurements; Semaphore.withPermit returns block R; telemetry records operation/outcome/duration; validators return typed success/failure.
Measure allocations, boxing, reflection, lock/dispatcher contention, GC, startup, artifact size, and compiler time with target-specific tools.
JFR, async-profiler, JMH, Native/JS profilers, static analysis; related: Semaphore, serialization limits, dependency scanning.

tabs.label: Syntax & Example

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: data class includes primary-constructor properties in generated toString; secrets and regulated data can leak through routine logging.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Optimize only a measured bottleneck, preserve readable baselines, add regression benchmarks, and define capacity/telemetry budgets.

sections.title: Decision Guides, Troubleshooting & FAQ
sections.description: Use the smallest construct that makes ownership, effects, failure, and evolution clear.

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Selecting the most concise or most advanced feature without documenting its failure mode, lifecycle, or compatibility cost.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Prefer T? over Result for reasonless absence; regular class over data class for identity; enum for uniform constants; sealed type for payload variants; suspend for one async result; Flow for many.

callouts.title: Common mistake
callouts.text: Treating a metadata-version error as corrupted cache when the resolved library was compiled by an incompatible Kotlin compiler.

callouts.title: Best practice
callouts.text: Align versions before cleaning, inspect generated JVM signatures for clashes, use local vals for smart casts, and inspect Job/collector ownership for hangs.

callouts.title: Common mistake
